name: Falsifiability
statement: A theory is scientific only if it forbids something: if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
meaning: Falsifiability, or refutability, is Karl Popper's criterion for the scientific status of a theory: a theory is scientific if and only if it is falsifiable, that is, if it forbids certain observations and so makes risky predictions that could in principle be refuted by observation or experiment. A theory compatible with every conceivable observation, one that nothing could ever count against, is for Popper not scientific. Popper offered falsifiability as his solution to the demarcation problem, the problem of distinguishing genuine science from non-science and pseudoscience, and he proposed it in deliberate opposition to the verifiability and inductive-confirmation criteria favored by the logical empiricists. His model of good science was Einstein's general theory of relativity, which made the bold, risky prediction that light would be bent by gravity, a prediction that could have failed but was borne out by Eddington's 1919 eclipse observations. By contrast, Popper argued that Freud's psychoanalysis and Adler's individual psychology could seemingly explain any behavior whatever, and so were not testable, and that Marx's theory of history had degenerated, through ad hoc rescues, from an originally testable theory into an unfalsifiable one. Popper set out these ideas in Logik der Forschung of 1934, translated as The Logic of Scientific Discovery in 1959, and in Conjectures and Refutations of 1963.
mechanism: Falsificationism reconceives how science works and how to tell it apart from pretenders. Popper accepted David Hume's critique of induction and denied that science proceeds by piling up confirming instances; no number of observed white swans can prove that all swans are white, since the next one might be black. He built his philosophy on a logical asymmetry: although a universal generalization can never be conclusively verified by any finite body of evidence, a single genuine counterexample can refute it. Science therefore advances not by induction but by conjecture and refutation: scientists propose bold, informative conjectures that stick their necks out by forbidding certain outcomes, then try their hardest to refute them by severe tests. A theory that survives such attempts is not proven true but merely corroborated, shown to have withstood testing so far, and remains open to future refutation. The scientific value of a theory lies in its testability, its willingness to prohibit observations and so to risk being wrong; the more a theory forbids, the more testable and the better it is. On this view the mark of a pseudoscience is not that it is false but that it is unfalsifiable, cast so as to be compatible with anything that could happen, or repeatedly rescued from refutation by ad hoc modifications that reduce its testability. Demarcation thus turns on the logical form and the methodological handling of a theory, not on its subject matter.

examples.text: General relativity risked a specific prediction of light-bending, confirmed at the 1919 eclipse, Popper's model of testable science.
Popper held that Freud's and Adler's psychologies could explain any behavior at all, and so were not testable.
No number of white swans proves all swans are white, but one black swan refutes it, which is why falsification matters.

variants.name: Conjecture and refutation
variants.text: Popper's picture of science as bold conjectures subjected to severe attempts at refutation, never verified but only corroborated.

variants.name: Degeneration into pseudoscience
variants.text: Popper's view that a theory like Marxism can slide from testable to unfalsifiable through ad hoc immunizing moves.

whyItMatters: Falsifiability is one of the most influential ideas in the philosophy of science and has shaped how scientists, educators, courts, and the public think about what makes an inquiry scientific. Popper's proposal reframed the demarcation problem, offering a clear and memorable test, does the theory forbid anything, that cut against the then-dominant idea that science is marked by accumulated confirmations. It gave a principled reason to distrust doctrines that explain everything and predict nothing, and it dignified boldness and testability as scientific virtues. The criterion has had real practical reach, invoked in debates over creationism and pseudoscience and in disputes about the standing of theories from economics to psychoanalysis. Popper's associated picture of science as conjecture and refutation, in which theories are never proven but only tentatively corroborated and always exposed to refutation, remains a powerful antidote to dogmatism and a natural expression of the fallibilist, self-correcting spirit of inquiry. Even critics who reject naive falsificationism take Popper's criterion as their starting point. As the idea that a theory earns scientific status by risking refutation, falsifiability is a landmark of twentieth-century thought about science.

working.text: check whether the theory rules out any possible observation, so that something could count against it.
try to refute the theory with risky predictions rather than seeking confirmations.
treat a theory that survives testing as corroborated and still open to refutation, never as proven.

limits: Falsifiability in its naive form faces serious objections, several rooted in the Duhem-Quine problem. Because a hypothesis is never tested in isolation but only together with auxiliary assumptions about instruments and conditions, a failed prediction never tells us with certainty which element is at fault, so a falsification can always be deflected by blaming an auxiliary rather than the target theory, and there is always room for ad hoc rescue. Thomas Kuhn observed that scientists do not in fact abandon a governing theory at the first anomaly, and arguably should not, since promising theories often face unsolved problems early on. The theory-ladenness of observation complicates the idea of a clean refuting observation, since what we take ourselves to observe is shaped by theory. Popper himself refined the view, distinguishing scientific from ad hoc modifications and developing notions of corroboration and degrees of testability, and later philosophers such as Lakatos tried to repair falsificationism. Whether probabilistic and statistical hypotheses can be strictly falsified, and whether the criterion is entirely adequate, remain debated. So falsifiability robustly captures a genuine mark of science, understood as a criterion whose naive form is complicated by the Duhem-Quine problem, ad hoc rescue, and the persistence of anomalies.
misreadings: Falsifiability is not the claim that scientific theories are false, but that they must be refutable in principle, capable of clashing with some possible observation. It is not verificationism, since Popper denied that theories are ever verified or proven, holding they are only corroborated or falsified. And an unfalsifiable theory is not thereby meaningless or worthless, only unscientific by Popper's criterion, so treating falsifiability as branding science false, as a form of confirmation, or as a test of meaning, misreads Popper's demarcation criterion.
origin: Karl Popper's criterion, set out in Logik der Forschung (1934), that a theory is scientific if and only if it is falsifiable, proposed as a solution to the demarcation problem in opposition to inductive verification.

sources.text: Karl Popper, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — Popper's criterion of falsifiability as the demarcation of science from non-science, the rejection of induction and verification, conjecture and refutation, corroboration, the logical asymmetry between verification and falsification, and his treatment of Marxism, psychoanalysis, and Adlerian psychology.

Karl Popper: Philosophy of Science, Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy. — falsifiability as the mark of the scientific, the Einstein light-bending example, the degeneration of Marxism into an unfalsifiable theory through ad hoc rescues, and the criticisms including the Duhem-Quine problem and theory-ladenness.
